Many orphaned giant anteater pups in Brazil are still nursing when their mothers are killed in road collisions. At rehabilitation centers, caregivers bottle-feed them, provide around-the-clock care, and help them build strength for a possible return to the wild. Nat Geo Explorer @fernando.faciole spent three years documenting these young animals and the people caring for them.

Over the past few years, fishermen off Cape Cod in Massachusetts have noticed fish being reeled out of the water with bite-shaped chunks missing or, in some cases, just their heads remain. The reason why has now been caught on camera for the first time by National Geographic Explorer and photographer @brianskerry: the great white sharks are back. 

Known as depredation, this behavior is usually seen from above the water’s surface. By working with local charter boat captains and using a custom designed camera set-up that ensured the fishing lure stayed in the camera's frame, Skerry was able to see what this looks like underwater. Depredation is a sign that great whites are returning to these waters after nearly being driven to extinction, shark conservationists worry the behavior could drive a new outbreak of human-shark conflict. 

Learn more about this rarely seen shark behavior and what it could mean for sharks and fishermen at the link in bio.

On safari in the Pantanal, photographer @sandesh_kadur noticed a black vulture in the middle of the water. "I wasn't sure what was going on, so our amazing Boat Guide, Branco, veered towards the vulture. That’s when I saw a dead caiman floating on the water's surface. The single vulture that had landed on it was trying in desperation to feed on the carcass, but the log-rolling caiman proved to be quite the challenge—like trying to eat while on a treadmill."

New cat alert! A call from a wildlife sanctuary about a "weird cat" has led to the first new cat species discovered in over 100 years. Smaller than an average housecat and covered in leopard-like spots, the cat species—proposed name Leopardus tilcayo—lives in Bolivia’s Yungas forest ecoregion, and very little is known about its day-to-day life in the wild. Its discovery is redrawing the branches of the cat family tree, and researchers hope the methods used to identify it could be used to find even more new cat species around the world.

Learn more about this feline surprise at the link in bio.

Fishing guide Justin Dymond spends his nights taking bowfishers out on Florida's Crystal River. But he's not the only one hunting. Bottlenose dolphins gather around his boat, using its lights to find and flush prey from hiding places—the first documented partnership of this kind in the United States. The relationship has changed how Dymond sees the cetaceans he once considered competition, and after years of watching it develop, he turned to National Geographic Explorer Stefanie Gazda to better understand it.

Until 2025, only two adult Tyrannosaurus rex footprints had been found in the entire world—but high school teacher Kent Hups made history when he discovered the first adult T. rex trackway. Working with his close friend and National Geographic Explorer Tyler Lyson, the pair excavated a total of five footprints in North Dakota, each preserved as a 3D shape in the ancient rocks.

Commercial poaching killed more than 90 percent of black rhinos in Zimbabwe and across the rest of Africa, eventually leaving none in Matusadona National Park. More than 30 years after officials and conservationists worked to rescue the remaining rhinos in the Zambezi Valley, descendants of those animals have returned to the park. Photographer @marcuswestbergphotography documented their return—and quieter moments as they rested throughout the day.

Eight years ago, photographer Pete McBride @pedromcbride almost lost his Colorado home to a wildfire. This summer, he heads back to the flames. Across the American West, an intense fire season is stretching firefighting teams thin. In Colorado, the Gold Mountain Fire has burned over 38,000 acres, while the Aspen Acres Fire has surpassed over 100,000 acres and destroyed hundreds of homes. Decades of drought in the southwest, along with one of the worst snowpacks in recorded history this past winter in the seven-state Colorado River Basin, and record heat waves, have created the perfect conditions for wildfires to escalate.

Learn more about what it takes to capture a world on fire at the link in bio.

One day, Phil Gordon's house will fall 247 feet (75 meters) off a sheer cliff outside of Homer, Alaska. On the beach below, Pacific Ocean waves constantly eat away at the cliff, and the bedrock holding the entire bluff in place is unstable. But Gordon refuses to let his home fall—so he's moving the property to a safe distance back.

Due to launch on August 30, NASA's new Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is around 100 times more powerful than the Hubble Telescope. Utilizing elements from a former spy satellite, and named after NASA’s first chief of astronomy, Roman will capture light from millions of galaxies and stars as it peers towards the galactic center. National Geographic was invited to NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland to see it firsthand and learn how they plan to use it to investigate dark energy and dark matter.

Learn more about how Roman could help solve the universe's greatest mysteries at the link in bio.

Giraffes may have more going for them besides their impressive height. 🦒

In a cognitive test, some giraffes successfully determined which sealed container held the larger total of carrots after more were added. The findings suggest these mammals may have strong numerical abilities that, while difficult to compare directly, could exceed those reported for dogs, horses, and zebrafish in similar studies. Researchers are now exploring what those abilities could reveal about giraffes in the wild.

Marine ecologist and National Geographic Explorer Brian Timmer (@scuba_timmer) uncovered evidence that bull kelp forests in the Salish Sea began collapsing long before climate change was widely recognized or discussed. What Timmer and his team found reframes the timeline of ocean warming and raises urgent questions about what else we may already have lost.

As the moon's shadow swept across Europe on August 12, the continent saw its first total solar eclipse in 27 years—but nowhere had a view quite as dramatic as Spain. National Geographic photographer @renan_ozturk set out to capture the moment in a different way. After months of preparation alongside @chrisburkard and @chris_sharma, the trio documented the moon passing over the sun as Sharma took on a deep-water solo climb in Mallorca, showcasing years of dedication through a once-in-a-lifetime shot.

Earlier this year, an FDA trial began for a potential glaucoma treatment. Called ER-100, and co-developed by molecular biologist David Sinclair, it aims to return damaged optic nerves to a more youthful state. But it could rewind the clock on any type of cell, making it the latest step in an accelerating race to redefine how our bodies age. D.T. Max (@dtmax_newyorker) explores more, including what it might take to make us younger, forever at the link in bio.

Video by Reuben Wu (@reuben). Totality from 7,303ft over the Sierra de Urbión, Soria, Spain, August 12, 2026. Eight months of work led to this moment. Maps, cloud climatology, permit rules, and a location shortlist. The final call on this spot came only two days ago, after 3 days of location scouting.

I wanted the eclipse as an integral part of the landscape rather than isolated against black sky. The eclipse about 7.5 degrees above the horizon — low enough that the whole atmosphere became the subject, the shadow sweeping across the terrain rather than simply overhead.

The thing no amount of planning prepares you for is how it feels. Temperature drops, birds go quiet, and then two minutes that pass like ten seconds. I’ve chased eclipses before, but it doesn’t get less astonishing. Sharing this experience with friends who came a long way to see it made it something else again.

Video by @joelsartore | Did someone say 18k? I’m thrilled to announce the 18,000th species to join the Photo Ark: the red handfish. As its name implies, this species belongs to a family of fish that walk with their oversize “hands” rather than swim. No bigger than my thumb, the handfish takes an entire year to cover a distance equivalent to that of a standard basketball court. It is considered one of the rarest fishes on Earth, with fewer than 250 individuals left in the wild. Habitat loss, pollution, climate change, and human disturbance are the main threats to the recovery of the red handfish population. This video was taken @imas_utas. To see more species featured in the Photo Ark, follow @joelsartore. #PhotoArk

Black rhinos once again roam Matusadona National Park, decades after poachers turned the Zimbabwean refuge into what one conservationist called “a killing zone for rhinos.” As commercial poaching killed more than 90 percent of the world's black rhinos, wildlife teams tracked survivors hiding in remote parts of the Zambezi Valley and hauled them through the bush on makeshift sleds until trucks could carry them to protected areas. More than 30 years later, some descendants of those survivors have returned to their ancestral landscape—and conservationists plan to release even more.

New drone footage from the Head of Bight, South Australia, shows a southern right whale mother resting belly-up, pectoral fins stretched into the air before slowly rotating to take a breath, then swiveling upside down again. They're the only large whale species documented doing this, but what's the purpose of this unusual behavior? Researchers now theorize it may be tied to energy conservation while nursing their calves, though there's another theory floating around.

Have you ever seen an organism made of glass? They're called diatoms, single-celled algae encased in silica. National Geographic Explorer @arielwaldman recovered her samples of these organisms from Antarctica, but they can be found around the world—and a microscope isn't the way to see them.
